transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. I'm Dr. [Your Name]. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Hi, doctor. Um… I came in because I really haven’t been sleeping, not properly, since the warehouse inspection. I keep thinking I’m going to be exhausted enough to just pass out, but then I’m lying there, staring at the ceiling, and these little pieces of it keep replaying in my head. Not even in order, just bits and sounds and flashes, and I can’t seem to make my brain stop doing it.

And when I do finally drift off, it doesn’t last. I wake up drenched in sweat and completely alert, like my body thinks I’m back there near that blast again. It’s… it’s really wearing me down. I know I probably sound scattered, but the sleep part is the thing that made me realize I couldn’t just keep trying to push through it.
Can you tell me more about the warehouse inspection and what happened during or after it that might be connected to how you're feeling now?

It was supposed to be routine, that’s the thing I keep getting stuck on. I was there for an inspection, just walking through the warehouse, looking at conditions and notes and all of that, and then… there was the explosion. I remember hearing it — like this huge crack and pressure all at once — and I remember that sound very clearly, too clearly.

But then there’s this gap. I can remember the explosion, and then the next clear thing I have is standing outside afterward with soot on my jacket. I keep trying to fill in the part between those two moments, like how I got out, who was near me, what I did, whether I ran or someone pulled me out or… I don’t know. It’s just blank. Not fuzzy exactly, more like there’s nothing there for me to grab onto.

And I’ve gone over it again and again in my head, because it feels like I should be able to remember. I mean, I was there. I’m the one who walked out somehow. But no matter how hard I try to piece it together, that whole middle part just isn’t there.
Since the explosion, have you found yourself avoiding places, people, or thoughts that remind you of what happened?

Yes… I have. More than I wanted to admit, honestly. At work I’ve been avoiding the warehouse file completely. It’s just sitting there, and I know I’m supposed to deal with it, or at least look at it, but even seeing the subject line in my email makes my stomach just drop. Like this sudden heavy feeling, and then I’ll click away or close the whole window.

And it’s not only that specific file. Calls about industrial accounts have started going to voicemail because I can’t make myself pick up. I tell myself I’ll call them back when I’m calmer or when I’ve had coffee or when I’ve “caught up” on something else, but really I just don’t want to hear anything that puts me back in that setting. Even opening emails that look like they might be related to warehouses or inspections makes me feel like I’m bracing for something. So yes, I guess I’m avoiding it. I keep trying to make it sound like I’m just behind on work, but I know it’s more than that.
Since the explosion, have you noticed any ongoing feelings of fear, anger, or emotional numbness, especially when you think about what happened or are reminded of it?

I’m… not totally sure how to answer that. I mean, I know I don’t feel normal, exactly, but when you say fear or anger or numbness, I don’t know that I can neatly point to one and say, yes, that’s what’s happening.

Sometimes when I’m reminded of it, I mostly just feel kind of unsettled and tense, like I don’t want to stay with the thought long enough to find out what the feeling is. It’s not like I sit there thinking, “I’m afraid,” in a clear way. And I haven’t really noticed being angry in any consistent way either. Maybe frustrated with myself, but I don’t know if that’s what you mean.

The numbness part… I’m not sure. There are moments where I feel kind of blank, but I don’t know if that’s emotional numbness or just me trying not to think about it too much. I guess I’m having a hard time separating it all out.

Since the explosion, have you noticed any persistent negative thoughts about yourself, the world, or the future—like thinking you’re helpless, or that the world is dangerous, or that something bad is always going to happen?

I don’t know that I’ve noticed that in a clear, constant way. Like, I’m not walking around thinking, “The world is dangerous,” or “Something bad is definitely going to happen,” at least not in those exact words.

I do catch myself being more cautious, I guess, but I’m not sure if that’s the same thing as believing everything is unsafe. It’s more like… when something reminds me of the warehouse, my mind kind of shuts the door on it before I can get too far into what I think about it. So if there are bigger thoughts underneath, I don’t know that I’ve really let myself look at them.

And I wouldn’t say I think I’m helpless, exactly. I mean, I feel frustrated that I can’t just handle things the way I normally would, but that feels different from believing I’m helpless as a person. I’m still going to work, still doing some things. Just not… not everything well.

So I guess my answer is: not really, or at least not that I can identify. I haven’t had one persistent thought like that that keeps repeating. It’s more avoidance and discomfort than a clear belief about myself or the whole world.
Have you noticed feeling down, irritable, or uninterested in things you usually enjoy most days since the explosion?

I don’t know if I’d say “down” exactly, or uninterested… I’m not sure. But irritable, yes. That has definitely been happening, and I hate admitting that because I don’t think of myself as someone who takes things out on people.

There was this moment at work where a junior analyst asked me a pretty small question about a spreadsheet. It wasn’t even a bad question, honestly. It was the kind of thing I normally would just answer or walk them through for two minutes. But I just… snapped. I answered way too sharply, like they’d done something wrong, and I could hear my tone as it was happening, but I still didn’t soften it enough. Afterward I felt really embarrassed, because that’s not how I usually treat people, especially someone newer who’s just trying to make sure they’re doing it right.

So, yes, irritability at least. I don’t know if it’s most days, exactly, but it’s been enough that I’ve noticed it, and that incident really stuck with me.
Since the explosion, have you noticed yourself being more on edge, easily startled, or constantly watchful, like you’re expecting something dangerous to happen?

Yes. That one I can answer more clearly. I’ve been jumpy in a way that feels… honestly kind of ridiculous when I say it out loud, because the things setting me off are normal office things.

Like if the printer jams and makes that sudden grinding noise, I jump like something really bad just happened. Or if a door slams down the hall, even if I know people come in and out all day, my whole body reacts before I can think. The worst is when someone comes up behind my desk and says my name or asks me a question—I’ll flinch or jerk around like they snuck up on me on purpose, even though they didn’t.

And it’s not just a quick little startle and then I’m fine. It takes me a few minutes to calm back down. I’ll sit there trying to act normal, but my heart is going and I feel tense, like my body hasn’t gotten the message that it was just a printer or a door or a coworker. It’s embarrassing, especially at work, because I don’t want people noticing that I’m reacting that strongly to ordinary noises.
Since the explosion, have you had any unwanted memories, nightmares, or sudden feelings of reliving the event, even when you don’t want to?

Yes… during the day, mostly. I wouldn’t say it’s like I sit there choosing to think about it, because I really don’t want to. It just kind of breaks in.

I’ll be at work, doing something completely ordinary—reviewing a policy or reading through a loss report—and suddenly I’ll get this really sharp image in my head of the worker on the floor. And the soot in the air. It’s not like I’m calmly remembering it, if that makes sense. It comes in fast and vivid, and my body reacts before I can stop it. Like my stomach drops, or I tense up, and for a second I’m not really with the document in front of me anymore.

Then I’m trying to pull myself back and act like nothing happened, because I’m at my desk and I’m supposed to be working. But it’s hard because it feels so immediate, like the image is right there again even though I know I’m not actually back there. It’s embarrassing, too, because there’s no outward reason for me to suddenly freeze or lose my place in what I’m reading.

So, yes, unwanted memories for sure. I don’t know how else to describe it except that they hit me out of nowhere.
